metaDescription: Six key finders for Android phones compared on ring volume, battery life, water rating and network, from Google Find Hub tags to Samsung and Tile options.
introParagraphs: An Android key finder is a Bluetooth tag that rings from an app on your phone and, when your keys are far away, shows a last known location through a network of nearby phones. Which network the tag uses matters more than any other spec. Google Find Hub, Samsung SmartThings Find and Tile each work differently, and a tag built for one will not pair with another.

We evaluated six tags based on product specs and buyer feedback: the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2, the Life360 Tile, the XJQX 2 pack, the AMZSMT 4 pack, the coioc dual-system 4 pack and the KIUP 4 pack. We compared stated ring volume, battery life, water rating, range and network, and we flagged where a listing gives no figures.
Use the tables below to match a tag to your phone and your habits, and remember that none of these is a GPS tracker.

products.badge: Best Loud Google Find Hub Tag
products.name: XJQX Android Tracker Tags, 2 Pack, 105 dB
products.description:
The XJQX is a two-pack of Android tags that work with Google Find Hub through the Find My Device app. The listing states a 105 dB alarm, the loudest figure for a Find Hub tag in this group, and a Bluetooth range of 350 ft. It says there is no subscription and no extra app.

The pack includes a black tag and a white tag so couples can tell theirs apart, plus two silicone keyring cases. Two spare CR2032 batteries come in the box on top of the two pre-installed ones, and the listing says each cell lasts more than 2 years. The tradeoff is that it covers Android only, and the claimed battery life of 2 years or more is a manufacturer figure.

It makes a neat gift for two people because each has their own color. Setup is a one-tap pairing with an Android phone. Compared with the AMZSMT at 80 to 100 dB, the XJQX is louder, and against the KIUP at 98 dB it adds a longer stated range but comes as two tags rather than four.
products.bestFor: Android couples who want a very loud Find Hub tag each.
pros: Stated 105 dB alarm is the loudest Find Hub tag here
Spare CR2032 cells and silicone cases are included
Black and white tags make it easy to tell yours apart
No subscription or extra app beyond Google Find Hub
cons: Android only, with no support for iPhone
Only two tags per pack, fewer than the 4 packs here
Battery claim of 2 years or more is a manufacturer figure

products.name: Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2 Bluetooth Tracker

specList.label: Battery
specList.value: Up to 500 days, CR2032 not included

specList.label: Alert
specList.value: Ring the tag from the app

products.description:
The Galaxy SmartTag2 is Samsung's redesigned tag, registered through SmartThings Find. The listing states an IP67 rating for water and dust, and a battery that lasts up to 500 days, or up to 40 percent more in non power saving mode. When your item is close, Search Nearby uses Compass View to guide you, and you can ring the tag if you still cannot see it.

It uses a replaceable CR2032 battery that is not included, so budget for a cell on day one. The tradeoff is that it is built around Samsung's own SmartThings Find system, so check that your phone supports it before buying. The listing does not give ring volume.

If your household is on Samsung phones, the SmartTag2 is the most natural fit. It also activates compatible smart home devices. Compared with the XJQX at 105 dB, the Samsung states no volume, but it adds a stated IP67 rating that the XJQX lacks, and against the KIUP at IP65 it has a stronger water rating.
products.bestFor: Samsung Galaxy owners who want a waterproof tag in their own ecosystem.
pros: IP67 rating handles rain, splashes and brief dunks
Battery lasts up to 500 days, per the listing
Compass View guides you to a nearby item
Uses a standard replaceable CR2032 coin cell
cons: CR2032 battery is not included in the package

products.name: AMZSMT Android Tracker Tags, 4 Pack, Find Hub
products.description:
The AMZSMT is a four-tag set that works with Google Find Hub on Android 9 and above, with no monthly fee. Turn on Bluetooth, hold the tag near the phone and follow the on-screen prompts. Nearby Search shows your distance within about 120 ft, and the built-in speaker is stated at 80 to 100 dB.

Each tag has a lanyard and can be shared through Find Hub so family members can help locate items. The listing says the battery is replaceable and lasts up to 2 years. The tradeoff is the wide volume range, which makes the real loudness uncertain, and that it is for Android only.

Four tags cover keys, a wallet, a backpack and a pet collar. Add each to the Find Hub app right after unboxing. Against the XJQX at 105 dB the AMZSMT is quieter at its upper end, but it gives four tags rather than two, and against the coioc it avoids dual-system pairing quirks.
products.bestFor: Android households that want several Find Hub tags with no subscription.

products.name: KIUP Android Tracker Tags, 4 Pack, 98 dB, UWB
products.description:
The KIUP is a four-tag Find Hub set with a speaker stated at up to 98 dB and an Ultra Wideband feature that shows your distance to the tag within Bluetooth range. The listing says it is for Android only, and it states it does not support Huawei phones. Four protective cases come in the pack.

It is rated IP65 for rain and splashes and the battery is said to last up to 2 years. The tradeoff is that the IP65 rating is lower than the IP67 on the Samsung and the coioc, and the Ultra Wideband distance view will only help on phones that support it. The listing does not say which phones those are.

If you struggle to pinpoint a hidden tag, a distance readout can speed the last few meters. Check your phone model before buying. At 98 dB it is a little quieter than the XJQX at 105 dB, but at IP65 it is better protected than the AMZSMT, which states no rating.
products.bestFor: Android users who want a loud four-pack with a distance readout.
pros: Speaker stated at up to 98 dB for hidden tags
Ultra Wideband distance view helps the last few meters
IP65 rating handles rain and splashes outdoors
Four tags and four cases come in one pack
cons: IP65 is a weaker rating than the IP67 on other tags
Not for Huawei phones, according to the listing
Distance view may depend on phone support the listing omits

products.name: coioc Air Tracker Tags, 4 Pack, Android or iOS

specList.label: Network
specList.value: Find Hub or Find My, one at a time

products.description:
The coioc four-pack is certified for both Google Find Hub on Android and Apple Find My on iPhone, so one set suits a mixed household. Within about 120 ft you can sound the built-in speaker from the app. The listing states an IP67 rating that handles splashes and brief immersion, and a replaceable battery.

Tags can be shared with family members, and the listing is clear that a tag cannot pair with both Android and iOS at the same time. The tradeoff is that mixed pairs still need separate tags, and the listing gives no ring volume or battery life figure. It is the most flexible pack for a household that might switch phones.

When you move from one platform to the other you have to reset the tag, so plan for that. Four tags give room to spread across keys, bags and luggage. Against the AMZSMT, which is Android only, the coioc adds iPhone support, and against the KIUP's IP65 it adds IP67.
products.bestFor: Households with both Android and iPhone users, or people who might switch.

cons: A tag pairs with only one network at a time

products.badge: Best for Mixed Phones and Family
products.name: Life360 Tile Bluetooth Tracker, iOS and Android
products.description:
The Life360 Tile works on both Android and iPhone through its own free app, and it is sold as a 1, 2 or 4 pack. You can ring the tag from the app, follow it on a map, or press the tag to ring your phone, even if the phone is silenced. It attaches to keys, bags or a water bottle.

It also includes a discreet SOS alert for notifying loved ones, and it connects to Life360 so family members and tagged items show on one map. The listing does not state ring volume, water resistance or battery type, so we cannot rank it on those points. The extras are only useful if the family uses Life360.

Tile uses its own network instead of Find Hub or SmartThings Find, so it does not rely on Google or Samsung phones nearby. A single tag on the main key ring is a sensible start. Compared with the XJQX at 105 dB, the Tile states no volume, but unlike the Samsung SmartTag2 it works on any Android phone and on iPhone as well.
products.bestFor: Families who mix Android and iPhone and want one shared app.

Life360 link shows family and items on one map

buyingCriteria.explanation: An Android tag is only as good as the network behind it. The XJQX, AMZSMT and KIUP use Google Find Hub, the Samsung SmartTag2 uses SmartThings Find, the Tile uses its own network, and the coioc supports Find Hub or Find My, one at a time. Far-away finding depends on nearby phones on that network. Check your phone supports the network before you buy.

A quiet tag is hard to find under a cushion. The XJQX states 105 dB, the KIUP up to 98 dB, and the AMZSMT 80 to 100 dB. The Samsung SmartTag2, coioc and Tile give no figure. Pick the XJQX if you lose keys in noisy rooms, and test the ring when it arrives.

Replaceable coin cells keep a tag alive for years, but listings differ. The Samsung lists up to 500 days on a CR2032 that is not included, the AMZSMT and KIUP up to 2 years, and the XJQX more than 2 years with spare cells in the box. The Tile and coioc give no figure. Check the app for a low battery warning.

Keys get rained on. The Samsung SmartTag2 and coioc state IP67, the KIUP states IP65, and the XJQX, AMZSMT and Tile state no rating. IP67 handles splashes and brief immersion, while IP65 handles rainwater and splashes. If your keys live outdoors, favor the Samsung or coioc.

More tags let you cover keys, a wallet, a bag and a pet. The AMZSMT, KIUP and coioc come as four packs, the XJQX as two, the Samsung as one, and the Tile as 1, 2 or 4. The AMZSMT, coioc and XJQX also support sharing. Count your items before choosing a pack size.

These are Bluetooth tags, not GPS trackers. They ring when near and rely on other phones to report a far-away location. In a quiet area that location can be old. The Samsung and KIUP add guidance within range, but none of these stops a theft.

howWeEvaluated.title: Network and compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which network each tag uses and which phones it supports. The XJQX, AMZSMT and KIUP use Google Find Hub, the Samsung uses SmartThings Find, the coioc supports Find Hub or Find My, and the Tile works on iOS and Android. Clear compatibility statements counted heavily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ring volume and finding aids
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated volume and tools for the last few meters. The XJQX claims 105 dB, the KIUP up to 98 dB with Ultra Wideband distance, and the Samsung offers Compass View. All figures are manufacturer claims, so we used them as relative guides.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at listed battery plans. The Samsung states up to 500 days, the AMZSMT and KIUP up to 2 years, and the XJQX includes spare CR2032 cells. We treated unstated life, as on the coioc and Tile, as unknown.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated water ratings. The Samsung and coioc state IP67, the KIUP IP65, and the others none. A stated rating earned more trust than a silent listing, though none of these was a guarantee.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each pick by what it does best. The XJQX leads on volume, the Samsung on IP67 and SmartThings, the AMZSMT on four-pack Find Hub value, the KIUP on distance finding, the coioc on dual-system flexibility and the Tile on mixed phones. We did not rank on popularity or review counts.

howToChoose.subheading: Google Find Hub vs Other Networks
howToChoose.intro: The network behind the tag decides how well far-away finding works.

cards.label: Google Find Hub
cards.text: The tag reports its location through nearby Android phones. The XJQX, AMZSMT, KIUP and coioc work this way. Choose one if you use a typical Android phone and want a wide crowd network.

cards.label: SmartThings Find or Tile
cards.text: The Samsung SmartTag2 uses Samsung's SmartThings Find, and the Life360 Tile uses its own Tile network. Choose the Samsung if you use a Galaxy phone, and the Tile if your home mixes phone types.

howToChoose.note: A tag cannot join two networks at once, so decide before you set it up.

faq.q: What is the best key finder for Android?
faq.a: For a Samsung Galaxy phone, the SmartTag2 states IP67 and a battery of up to 500 days. For other Android phones, the XJQX stands out at 105 dB and the AMZSMT offers four Find Hub tags. If your home mixes phones, the Tile or the coioc is more flexible.

It is Google's network for finding tagged items using nearby Android devices. Tags like the XJQX, AMZSMT and KIUP report to it. You ring the tag from the app when it is near, or check a last known location when it is far.

faq.q: Can I use an Apple AirTag with Android?
faq.a: Not for setup, since Apple tags are built for Find My and iOS. If you want one set for both phone types, choose the coioc, which supports Find Hub or Find My, or the Tile. Remember that a tag pairs with only one network at a time.

faq.q: Do these tags need a subscription?
faq.a: The AMZSMT and XJQX state no subscription is required for Find Hub. The other listings do not state a fee. Check the app screen before paying for anything extra.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: The Samsung lists up to 500 days, the AMZSMT and KIUP up to 2 years, and the XJQX more than 2 years per cell with spares in the box. The coioc and Tile give no figure. Replace the cell as soon as the app warns you.

faq.q: Are Android key finders the same as GPS trackers?
faq.a: No, and this is the most common misconception. A tag rings by Bluetooth when it is close and relies on other phones to report a last known location. In a quiet area that location can be old, and a tag cannot stop a theft.
